FAST

SYDNEY, Nov 26 : Australian business investment surged anew in the September quarter as firms poured money into data centres, recording its biggest rise since 2011 at the height of the mining boom, while companies further upgraded spending plans for coming months. The strong numbers on Thursday suggested some resilience in the Australian economy even as five interest rate hikes this year triggered the biggest housing downturn in 40 years, hit consumer spending and weakened the labour market. The local dollar rose 0.2 per cent to $0.6640 and three-year government bond futures reversed earlier gains to be down three ticks to 95.51. The Australian Bureau of Statistics reported private capital spending jumped 12.2 per cent in the third quarter to an inflation-adjusted A$59.5 billion ($39.37 billion), far above market forecasts of a 4.4 per cent rise.  That was led by an 87 per cent jump in spending on information media and telecommunications equipment amid record investment in server racks and processing gear for data centres. Much of this was on imported equipment and thus an offsetting drag on economic growth.

Abhijit Surya, senior APAC economist at Capital Economics, said spending on information and communications technology could nearly double in the 2027 financial year, in contrast with the rest of the economy, where capital spending was struggling to tread water. "With the RBA clearly concerned about capacity pressures, the data suggest it won’t be in a rush to cut rates anytime soon," Surya said.  Markets are still wagering that the next move in interest rates will be down, but do not fully price a first cut from the Reserve Bank of Australia until August. A June cut is now seen as an 83 per cent chance. Overall spending on plant and machinery shot up 23.1 per cent, while spending on buildings and structures rose 1.7 per cent. An ABS survey of firms showed they planned to spend A$223.7 billion in the year to June 2027, 11.8 per cent higher than the previous estimate. ($1 = 1.5113 Australian dollars)

FAST

TOKYO, Nov 26 : The Bank of Japan must respond swiftly to signs of an inflation overshoot, including by accelerating the pace of interest rate hikes, hawkish board member Naoki Tamura said on Thursday, keeping alive prospects of a rate increase as soon as December. Rising raw material costs, including from higher crude oil prices due to the Middle East conflict, are already pushing up prices for a wide range of goods with the pass-through to consumer inflation seen intensifying ahead, Tamura said. "Recent price developments suggest further upside risks to inflation," he said, warning of price pressures from the Middle East war, higher import costs from a weak yen and still-robust demand for AI-related goods. "Given that financial conditions remain accommodative, I believe the BOJ needs to bring its policy rate to a level deemed neutral to the economy soon," Tamura said in a speech.

The remarks come ahead of the BOJ's two-day policy meeting ending on December 18, when markets widely expect the central bank to raise its policy rate to 1.5 per cent from the current 1.25 per cent. They also highlight the BOJ's focus on inflation risks, even as the recent market volatility and soft consumption cloud the outlook for Japan's fragile economy. Tamura said financial conditions remained accommodative with surveys suggesting the BOJ's past rate hikes, and potential future increases, were unlikely to inflict huge damage on corporate activity. "Within a few months of each rate hike, the BOJ can make a reasonable assessment of financial conditions" based on various surveys, Tamura said, signalling scope to follow up a rate hike in September with another one as soon as next month. "Given that underlying inflation in Japan is less firmly anchored at the BOJ's 2 per cent target, I believe the BOJ must respond swiftly to signs of an upward deviation in prices, including by accelerating the pace of policy interest rate hikes," he said. STILL SOME WAY TO NEUTRAL With high energy costs and the weak yen adding to inflationary pressures, the BOJ raised its policy rate to 1.25 per cent in September after delivering a hike in June — a shorter interval than the roughly twice-a-year hikes seen in 2024 and 2025.  The central bank kept rates steady in October, but said underlying inflation has roughly hit its 2 per cent target and signalled its readiness to continue hiking rates to prevent price growth from accelerating too much. Tamura did not mention an estimate he made in the past putting Japan's neutral rate, or the level that neither cools nor overheats the economy, around 2 per cent. But he said the BOJ's policy rate was "still some way" from neutral when judging from still-loose financial conditions. The need for further rate hikes is heightened by the fact Japan's inflation expectations are less firmly anchored than in other economies, leaving underlying inflation more vulnerable to large swings from external shocks, he said. "In my view, the BOJ therefore must respond to shocks more swiftly and strongly than would be necessary if underlying inflation were anchored more firmly." A former commercial bank executive, Tamura, along with former bond strategist Hajime Takata, is seen by markets as among the hawks on the nine-member board who prefer to hike rates steadily to forestall the risk of too-high inflation.

Source: Reuters

FAST

SEOUL, Nov 26 : The Bank of Korea raised its benchmark interest rate on Thursday, resuming its tightening cycle and upgrading its 2027 growth outlook to the fastest in six years amid a chip-driven export boom and persistent inflation. The move aligns the BOK with other emerging market economies, which are grappling with persistent commodity and supply pressures linked to the war in the Middle East. The seven-member monetary policy board voted to raise the 7-day repurchase rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 3.25 per cent, its highest since November 2024, a decision forecast by 32 of 34 analysts surveyed by Reuters. The bank also raised this year's growth forecast to 3.9 per cent from 3.3 per cent previously, and took its August outlook of 2.9 per cent for next year to 4.1 per cent, the fastest since 2021.

South Korea's policy-sensitive three-year treasury bond futures extended losses after the policy statement, falling 0.24 points to 103.77. The bank also saw stickier inflation for 2027, at 2.4 per cent, up from 2.3 per cent previously. "The central bank’s main concern is inflation, which has remained above its 2 per cent target since the conflict in Iran began – it came in at 2.8 per cent from a year ago in October," Gareth Leather, an analyst at Capital Economics, said after the rate decision. "Rapidly rising property prices, particularly in Seoul, could strengthen the case for a more prolonged tightening cycle." The hike was the BOK's third this year, following back-to-back increases in July and August, and brought cumulative tightening to 75 basis points. Asia's fourth-largest economy has expanded faster than anticipated in 2026 on surging global demand for semiconductors. Policymakers remained on a hawkish footing due to a heated housing market and headline inflation hovering well above the BOK's 2 per cent target. At its previous meeting on October 22, the central bank held rates steady at 3.00 per cent to assess external risks and the lagging impact of its summer hikes, while sharply upgrading its economic growth projections for both this year and next. BOK Governor Shin Hyun Song, who last month said the bank will take a data-dependent approach rather than a fixed rate trajectory, is scheduled to hold a news conference at 0210 GMT to explain the board's decision.

Source: Reuters

Nov 26 : Australia's Flight Centre Travel said on Thursday it was investigating unusual activity in a third-party accommodation booking system that may have exposed a significant number of customer records, pushing its shares down 2 per cent. Shares of the travel retailer fell as much as 2.1 per cent to A$10.64 in early trade, hitting their weakest level since October 19. • Flight Centre said some of its leisure travel brands — the Flight Centre brand, Travel Associates and Cruiseabout — and some independent agents used the third-party accommodation booking system. Nov 25 : Dimorphos, the small asteroid struck by NASA's DART spacecraft in 2022 in the first test of a planetary defense system, was left with one side flattened with a stadium-sized crater and is tumbling in space, as shown by images taken by the European Space Agency's Hera spacecraft released on Wednesday. DART was sent on a proof-of-principle mission for using a spacecraft to change a celestial object's trajectory. Dimorphos, an oblong-shaped rocky object about 495 feet (151 meters) wide, orbits its companion asteroid Didymos, with a diameter of 2,395 feet (730 meters), and the pair is currently about 120 million miles (193.5 million km) from Earth. They are defined as near-Earth asteroids, though neither object imperils Earth. Previous data showed how DART succeeded in changing the path of Dimorphos — demonstrating that a spacecraft could alter the trajectory of an object headed toward a collision with Earth. Hera is now getting a close-up look at how DART physically changed Dimorphos. "The side impacted is now completely covered by a crater, with the visual impression that a piece of the asteroid was cut off by the impact. We do not see evidence for major changes on the site opposite to the DART impact. The combination of those two observations is surprising," Michael Kueppers, ESA's Hera mission scientist, told Reuters.

The big crater covers nearly the whole front side of Dimorphos as it continues its orbit of Didymos.  "Dimorphos is now tumbling in a chaotic way. There are hundreds of boulders floating around in the system," Kueppers said. Hera, about the size of a small car, is presently observing Didymos and Dimorphos from a distance of about 15 to 19 miles (25 to 30 km). Hera next month is slated to approach within 8 miles (13 km) of the pair, obtaining increasingly higher-resolution images.  In January, Hera is due to deploy two shoebox-sized miniature satellites, called CubeSats, that will approach even closer for further study, including investigating the interior structure of the two asteroids. Hera's mission manager unveiled the new images at a dinosaur hall in the Museum für Naturkunde Berlin as a reminder of the danger of asteroid impacts like the one 66 million years ago that caused a mass extinction on Earth and doomed the dinosaurs. The DART, short for Double Asteroid Redirection Test, spacecraft collided with Dimorphos on September 26, 2022, at about 14,000 miles per hour (22,530 kph). "We knew that the DART mission impacted Dimorphos successfully and that it changed its orbit. But we did not know what happened to Dimorphos itself. The investigation of what the impact did to Dimorphos and the characterization of it in general is needed to be able to apply the kinetic impactor technique to another asteroid, should we find one on a collision course with Earth," Kueppers said.

Source: Reuters

WASHINGTON, Nov 25 : The Federal Communications Commission is authorizing Elon Musk's SpaceX to deploy a constellation of 1 million satellites for data centers in space, the agency said on Wednesday. SpaceX earlier this year sought permission to deploy up to 1 million orbital compute modules to process massive amounts of data to be used on Earth. The FCC said it was approving the SpaceX “Starmind” constellation to help meet rapidly growing demand for AI computing. Under the license, SpaceX must begin deployment no later than November 2033, deploy 10 per cent of the maximum number — or 100,000 — no later than November 2035 and deploy 50 per cent by November 2038, the FCC said. Approving the application will permit SpaceX "to pioneer emergent technology that advances American leadership in space and artificial intelligence," the FCC added.

Data centers are the physical backbone of artificial intelligence, requiring massive amounts of power. "By directly harnessing near-constant solar power with little operating or maintenance costs, these satellites will achieve transformative cost and energy efficiency while significantly reducing the environmental impact associated with terrestrial data centers," SpaceX told the FCC. It was unclear whether SpaceX would put 1 million satellites in space, where only 17,000 satellites exist currently. Satellite operators sometimes request approval for higher numbers of satellites than they intend to deploy to buy design flexibility. SpaceX sought approval for 42,000 Starlink satellites before it began deployment of that system. The growing network currently has just over 11,000 satellites in space. SpaceX's request bets heavily on reduced costs of Starship, the company's next-generation reusable rocket under development, to help deploy satellites. Amazon's rival satellite unit Leo and others have criticized the plan, suggesting SpaceX was unlikely to deploy all the satellites and that it could take centuries to do so. FCC Chair Brendan Carr rejected that criticism in March. "Amazon should focus on getting Amazon's house in order with their own launches and their own satellite constellation, rather than worrying about other people that are actually out there launching satellites at the pace and cadence that SpaceX is," Carr said. The FCC said it was also approving SpaceX's requests to back up its optical network by approving additional communications.

NEW YORK: The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq retreated on Wednesday (Nov 25) amid a tech selloff, but finished well off the day's lows as bargain hunters stepped in ahead of the US Thanksgiving holiday. The Dow finished higher. The Nasdaq fell more than 4 per cent early in the session as the selloff in AI-related stocks and new US tariff proposals hit sentiment. "There are all these potential headwinds, but then there's also a certain amount of conditioning of buying on the dip, and that's part of what we're seeing," said Oliver Pursche, senior vice president and adviser for Wealthspire Advisors in Westport, Connecticut.

"The broad selloffs tend to kind of throw the baby out with the bathwater. Investors are taking advantage of some of those discrepancies," he said. Technology and consumer discretionary fell 1 per cent each and led declines among S&P 500 sectors, while materials and real estate led gainers . Value stocks outperformed growth, with the Russell 1000 value index up 0.4 per cent and the Russell 1000 growth index down 0.8 per cent. Wall Street has been roiled this month, partly because of worries about AI leader Nvidia. Jensen Huang resigned as CEO earlier this month, but the company's board reinstated him on Monday. The Nasdaq Composite is down 7.3 per cent for the month. "This has broadly been a more sentiment-driven type of selloff," said Charlie Ripley, senior investment strategist at Allianz Investment Management. At the same time, for some companies from a price-to-earnings perspective, "things are starting to look more attractive", he said. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 164.25 points, or 0.33 per cent, to 50,182.95, the S&P 500 lost 18.31 points, or 0.25 per cent, to 7,182.78 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 147.73 points, or 0.62 per cent, to 23,585.80. The market will be closed on Thursday and will close early on Friday.

AI WORRIES LINGER Nvidia shares fell 3.9 per cent and an index of semiconductors was off 0.7 per cent, while shares of Amazon fell 3.1 per cent. On the plus side, PC maker HP gained 11.5 per cent after it reported fourth-quarter revenue and profit above analysts' estimates. Fears of increased regulatory scrutiny of the AI sector following the Democratic sweep in the US midterm elections have added to worries about AI stocks . Early in the day, the Nasdaq 100 briefly fell 20 per cent from its record closing high, flirting with bear-market territory. New tariffs could cloud the outlook for investors grappling with the prospect of interest rates staying higher for longer, as inflation has accelerated and oil prices have risen steadily due to the Iran war. The US proposed tariffs on goods from 14 trading partners to combat what it calls structural excess industrial capacity, reviving global trade tensions In addition, investors digested data showing the US economy grew much faster than initially estimated in the third quarter, while inflation increased further in October, reinforcing expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise rates next month and again in early 2027. "Tariffs are somewhat responsible for inflation ... so that's actually being counterproductive to what the Fed is trying to do," said Peter Cardillo, chief market economist at Spartan Capital Securities in New York. Volume was lower than average for part of the session. Trading on US exchanges ended at about 22 billion shares.

Nov 25 : Anthropic's slide below its initial public offering price has sharpened investor scrutiny of lofty technology valuations, as markets increasingly question whether even the biggest beneficiaries of the AI boom can generate enough profit to justify their price tags. Shares of the Claude developer were trading around $80.50, well below their $83 offer price and nearly 30 per cent below their opening price on November 19. The swift reversal highlights growing unease over how much investors are willing to pay for future growth, even as earnings prospects improve for many companies benefiting from artificial intelligence. Of the 86 Nasdaq-100 companies with positive earnings multiples and available earnings revision data, 60 saw their forward 12-month earnings forecasts rise over the past three months, a Reuters analysis of LSEG data showed. Yet, shares in 37 of those companies declined over the same period.

Nvidia shares have fallen about 25 per cent over the past three months despite a nearly 20 per cent increase in its earnings forecasts, partly driven by the volatile swings around CEO Jensen Huang's abrupt exit and reinstatement, while Marvell Technology and Lumentum have each lost more than 40 per cent of their market value even as earnings estimates rose 15 per cent and 20 per cent, respectively. HIGH EXPECTATIONS Despite the selloff, substantial valuation premiums persist. The 25 most richly valued companies in the Nasdaq-100 — many with exposure to AI, autonomous driving and other emerging technologies — traded at a median of 38 times projected earnings for the next 12 months, compared with 18 times for the remaining companies with positive earnings multiples, Reuters calculations showed. Anthropic illustrates how much future growth is already embedded in technology share prices. Morningstar's fair value estimate of $92 per share, just 12 per cent above Anthropic's latest closing price, assumes its annual revenue will increase nearly sevenfold over the next five years. Morningstar's estimates range from $25 to $188 per share under different scenarios, underscoring how sensitive Anthropic's valuation is to assumptions about future growth and profitability. The reassessment of valuations has been uneven across the tech sector. Forward price-to-earnings multiples for cybersecurity firms Fortinet and Palo Alto Networks rose the most over the past three months, climbing 11.5 per cent and 10.8 per cent, respectively. Multiples for Sandisk, Nvidia, Intuit Inc and Analog Devices contracted the most, falling between 15 per cent and 26 per cent, LSEG data showed. "Investors pay up for earnings they believe will last and discount those they think will fade," said Christopher Gannatti, global head of research at asset manager WisdomTree. Gannatti contrasted Palantir's high valuation with memory-chip maker Micron's much lower multiple, arguing that high memory prices could spur additional supply and eventually depress prices and profits. Palantir trades at 65 times forward earnings, compared with just 3.5 times for Micron, LSEG data showed. THE COST OF GROWTH The cost of delivering the growth implied by these valuations is another threat to future profitability. CoreWeave reported a 168 per cent rise in third-quarter revenue to $3.66 billion and a contracted revenue backlog of $132.5 billion. Yet the AI computing provider recorded a net loss of $709 million and expects capital spending of $37 billion to $39 billion this year. "Technological breakthroughs don't automatically translate into attractive returns on capital," said Troy Hooper, co-head of equity capital markets for the Americas at Mergermarket. "A year ago, investors were paying a much bigger premium for the promise of AI. Today, they're getting more tangible evidence of that promise and are seeking stronger profits." Growing competition could push down AI prices for customers, to the detriment of the companies investing heavily in the technology, Hooper said. Willis Tsai, head of global equities at Nuveen, said rising depreciation charges on AI chips and servers could erode cloud companies' profit margins even as demand for computing capacity grows.

(Reporting By Patturaja Murugaboopathy, Editing by Vidya Ranganathan and Nia Williams)

Source: Reuters

The US Treasury Department is working with the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and third-party forensic examiners to determine the scope and impact, according to the official. Outages and disruptions across tech, government and other systems have become a growing concern for governments, companies and the public in recent months, as advanced AI tools make it easier to find vulnerabilities and attack systems.

LONDON, Nov 25 : Britain is advancing plans to open up BBC iPlayer to advertising and rival broadcasters, potentially paving the way for an overhaul of the streaming platform, according to two people with knowledge of the matter. The proposal would represent a significant expansion of iPlayer's role as a platform for BBC programmes, with one of the people saying the technology upgrade that would be required could cost tens of millions of pounds. The potential technology investment to allow iPlayer to carry advertising attached to content from rivals including Channel 4 has not been reported previously. It is part of wider efforts among British broadcasters to compete with global streaming services such as Netflix, Disney+ and Amazon Prime Video. The change is expected to feature in a White Paper on the BBC's charter renewal, due by the end of the year, setting out the government's position on the public broadcaster's funding, governance and remit from 2028, the two people said.

The BBC pointed to comments by Director General Matt Brittin, who in July said one opportunity for Channel 4 would be “in partnership with the BBC, having content on iPlayer, but continuing to be ad-funded". The BBC's current funding model is based on a licence fee paid by TV-watching households. The proposal could also potentially enable the BBC to carry advertising around some of its own content, something barred under its current charter, the first person added. The government said last year that one option under consideration was to allow advertising around older BBC iPlayer content. The investment could be funded by the BBC's commercial arm, with the funds recovered over time through fees charged to third-party content providers, the first person said. An upgrade to iPlayer would also allow UKTV, the BBC-owned commercial broadcaster that operates advertising-funded channels such as U&Drama and U&Dave, to integrate content into the platform, the two people said. Other broadcasters, including ITV, could join in time, the second person added, potentially creating a shared platform for a wider range of British television content. The plan echoes Project Kangaroo, a proposed joint streaming venture between the BBC, ITV and Channel 4 that was blocked by UK regulators in 2009. Since then, streaming services and YouTube have taken a growing share of viewing.  SHARED PLATFORM FOR BRITISH BROADCASTERS The British government told Reuters it was aware that Channel 4 and the BBC were open to collaboration and partnership. "We continue to support and encourage all public service media providers to explore strategic partnerships where they benefit their audiences and the sustainability of the public service media ecosystem as a whole," a Department for Culture, Media and Sport spokesperson said. "The BBC must be funded by a model that is sustainable and fair. Through the BBC Charter Review, we are looking at a range of options, including how the licence fee could be reformed, but no final decisions have been made." A BBC spokesperson said: "As we have said before, we believe increased collaboration between all public service broadcasters is vital to ensure the industry thrives in a highly competitive global marketplace." Channel 4 Chief Executive Priya Dogra told lawmakers this month that the iPlayer idea was "worth exploring" but said that details needed to be worked out, including how advertising would work. British broadcasters are increasingly distributing their content through rival platforms to reach new audiences. Channel 4 will make some programmes available on Disney+ next year while the BBC is testing CBeebies children's programming content on Netflix. British media regulator Ofcom said in July that 26 per cent of UK viewers turned to Netflix first when deciding what to watch, compared with 25 per cent for the BBC. In its March submission to the BBC Charter Review, the BBC proposed exploring the integration of UKTV into iPlayer while keeping it distinct from BBC-branded content and services.

Source: Reuters

AI stock rout deepens but damage is limited by afternoon bounce

FAST

Nov 25 : AI-linked stocks plunged early on Wednesday but staged an afternoon comeback, the latest autumn clash pitting investor concern about rising costs and forbidding debt dynamics against strong buying interest given the steep decline in prices. AI lab Anthropic traded as low as $73.85 shortly after the open, putting it 11 per cent below its initial offering price last week, before it rallied to close 1 per cent higher at $82.19. Alphabet dropped 4.7 per cent and hit a 52-week low before closing the gap to end down 2.1 per cent. Chip giant Broadcom, one of the leaders of an epic midyear semiconductor rally, dropped 5.8 per cent before ending flat. The Nasdaq Composite ended down 0.6 per cent after early trading off as much as 4.6 per cent. The Nasdaq-100 had a similar trajectory, closing down 0.6 per cent on the day after briefly flirting with a decline of 20 per cent from last month's high. Despite the rebound, the declines were the second straight daily drop in tech and reflected the unwind of earlier optimism in the AI sector, driven in part by Democratic wins in US midterm elections that promise greater regulation and a slower, costlier AI buildout. Sentiment was further impaired on Wednesday by the Trump administration's proposed new tariffs on imports from 14 trading partners and data showing US inflation increased further in October.

But the selling, which began soon after the Nasdaq Composite's record high on October 6 and increased markedly in the second half of November, also underscored gathering concern about the financial underpinnings of an infrastructure expansion that has increasingly been financed by large sales of debt — a practice that tends to make markets more fragile and vulnerable to reversal. Overnight in Tokyo, OpenAI shareholder SoftBank fell 14 per cent, underscoring fears that ChatGPT maker OpenAI may face increasing resistance as it seeks to raise money. SoftBank, also a major investor in chip firm Arm, is down more than 40 per cent for the year. Nvidia, a major OpenAI partner in data centers and other aspects of the AI ecosystem, dropped 8.5 per cent to a fresh low before ending 3.9 per cent lower. The so-called neocloud firms that back AI data center capacity were under renewed attack, reflecting in part concern about their capacity to raise funds to support ambitious building plans. "It seems that these companies are trying to one-up each other on the amount of money that they're spending, but you have to show that it's worth it, and that's where Wall Street is saying, 'I don't know'," said Todd Schoenberger, chief investment officer at CrossCheck Management. HEADING INTO BEAR TERRITORY The Nasdaq-100 briefly fell 20 per cent below its October 6 record closing high. The worries about the underpinnings of the AI boom were so significant that even firms reporting strong results were caught in the downdraft, reflecting in part their large stock-price gains earlier in the year. Dell Technologies fell 5.7 per cent early on Wednesday despite the server maker raising its annual revenue and profit forecasts for the third time this year and approving an additional $25 billion share buyback. Dell stock recovered to rise 0.6 per cent and has more than doubled for the year. Rival AI server maker HPE tumbled 16.3 per cent on Tuesday after raising its full-year revenue outlook. Shares of Ambarella, valued at $2 billion, tumbled 20.9 per cent after the AI semiconductor firm forecast fourth-quarter revenue below analysts' estimates. The Philadelphia chips index slid 7 per cent to hit a more than seven-month low before closing 0.6 per cent lower. The index has plunged more than 43 per cent from its record high in June. Shares of AI hyperscalers were broadly lower, with Oracle down 5 per cent and Amazon.com off 3 per cent. Nvidia-backed neocloud firms CoreWeave and Nebius Group fell more than 10 per cent each, before CoreWeave closed flat and Nebius down 2.7 per cent, while IREN, Applied Digital and Core Scientific were mostly narrowly mixed after early declines. Neocloud providers, which rent out specialized AI computing capacity, have been under pressure since October over concerns about the debt funding their rapid expansion. The yield on CoreWeave's bonds due 2031 rose to almost 18 per cent as prices fell nearly 2 cents on the dollar to near record lows, Tradeweb data showed. The cost of insurance against tech companies defaulting on debts has jumped sharply, with five-year CDS spreads at Oracle, Alphabet, SpaceX and CoreWeave hitting record levels.

Source: Reuters

FAST

MUMBAI, Nov 25 : Indian fintech PhonePe has resumed preparations for its initial public offering and is targeting a listing in the first three months of next year at a valuation of $12 billion to $15 billion, a person directly aware of the discussions said. The Walmart-backed company is expected to file its updated draft papers with India's market regulator, the Securities and Exchange Board of India, within the next 30 to 45 days, the person said, requesting anonymity as talks are confidential. The listing is set to be India's biggest fintech debut since Paytm's $2.5 billion float in 2021. PhonePe had paused its listing plans in March due to global capital market volatility stoked by geopolitical tensions in the Middle East. The issue will be an entirely secondary share sale to raise $1.2 billion to $1.5 billion, retaining the size outlined in PhonePe's January draft prospectus, where majority owner Walmart said it would trim its stake by about 12 per cent, and investors Tiger Global and Microsoft planned to fully exit.

PhonePe, the dominant player in digital payments in India with over 650 million registered users, processed nearly 11.4 billion of the country's 25.4 billion Unified Payments Interface (UPI) transactions in October. Indian business daily The Economic Times on Wednesday first reported PhonePe's plans to resume its IPO. Walmart and PhonePe didn't immediately respond to Reuters' email seeking comment. The Bengaluru-based fintech, which competes with Google Pay and Paytm in India, expects to turn profitable in the next fiscal year, excluding any fee revenue on UPI and government digital payments incentives, according to the person cited above. India bars banks and fintech platforms like PhonePe from charging fees on standard UPI transfers to encourage digital adoption. A government proposal to introduce a 0.4 per cent merchant fee on transactions exceeding 2,000 rupees ($21) was recently deferred indefinitely following opposition from retailers.
